direction.premise: A tabletop supersonic-flow instrument, with a luminous compressible-gas chamber and a dark oxide-steel control console.
direction.composition: A single illuminated visualization tank dominates the screen. Compact mechanical lab instruments occupy a side console on desktop and a vertically scrollable lower console on narrow phones.
direction.shapeLanguage: Hard square-cut aluminum geometry, paper-thin graduations, sharp instrument toggles and an uncaged central visualization.
direction.surfaceAndMaterial: Opaque charcoal-blue oxided metal; brushed mineral wall inclusions; the gas field itself provides dynamic luminous volume. No glassmorphism or decorative gradients over UI components.
direction.paletteLogic: Cool sea-glass blue denotes rarefaction, warm sulfur amber denotes compression, gray-yellow denotes impermeable walls. Controls follow the chamber's material scale.
direction.typography: Condensed utility labels with monospaced physical measurements; short Russian action labels remain readable on phones.
direction.signature: A finger can draw a reflecting mirror directly into the gas in real time, and the computed shock splits and wraps around its geometry.
direction.distinction: Where PetriForge is a discrete editable microcosm, SHOCK shows continuous conservation-law fronts and reflective solid boundaries with industrial instrumentation.

architecture.primaryVerb: Place a high-pressure impulse, alter the wall shape and measure where the front reaches.
architecture.physicalFeedback: The actual HLL field changes on each step, a brief excitation circle identifies the contact source, and wall edits appear immediately as solid reflective cells.
architecture.spatialRationale: The physical chamber gets the majority of the viewport; on a phone the lower control board scrolls internally without moving the live wave display.

comparisons.spatialDifference: PetriForge's tiled Petri grid is replaced by an uncaged fluid image and side instrument console.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Free-hand gas obstacle drawing and physical impulse propagation replace discrete agent rewards.

comparisons.spatialDifference: No paper studio, no painterly cards; industrial short-text control board framing a computational gas tank.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Direct injection and continuous waves replace turn-based drawing.

comparisons.spatialDifference: SHOCK uses a pressure-field instrument bay rather than the source project's discrete object geometry.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Gas impulse injection, boundary drawing and live pressure measurement have distinct controls and physical consequences.

production.renderer: Plain Canvas 2D with an offscreen 2D gas raster driven by a JavaScript conservative HLL finite-volume solver; responsive cell resolution.
production.focalAsset: Actual pressure, density and density-gradient fields, with a hand-authored pressure-trace SVG icon.

motion.character: Physical concentric shocks and interference emerge from conservation equations; the UI provides only brief source registration.
motion.action: Immediate impulse and instantaneous solid raster stroke.
motion.anticipation: The selected input tool and canvas crosshair reveal the pending effect.
motion.response: The numerical field reacts during subsequent solver steps and the click adds a minimal source marker.
motion.followThrough: Shock paths refract, diffract and reflect while live time/pressure measurements advance.
motion.interruption: Touch cancellation finishes the active edit and does not leave captured gestures; hiding pauses calculations.
motion.reducedMotion: Animations outside the physical field are removed; physical calculation remains manually pausable.

evidence.expectedChange: The computed gas pressure returns to ambient while walls remain visible.
